Series::clamp¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::clamp(double min_v, double max_v) const -> Series
Series& Series::clamp_(double min_v, double max_v)

What It Does¶

Applies a two-sided bound to every element in one call.

Conceptually, for each position i:

  • if self[i] < min_v, the result is min_v

  • if self[i] > max_v, the result is max_v

  • otherwise, the result is self[i] unchanged

This is the combined form of clamp_min() followed by clamp_max() — x.clamp(lo, hi) and x.clamp_min(lo).clamp_max(hi) produce the identical result, in one call instead of two. clamp() returns a new series; clamp_() mutates the current series in place and returns Series&.

Important

min_v must not exceed max_v min_v > max_v throws immediately, before any element is touched — there is no implicit swap or silent reinterpretation of the bounds. See Example 4.

Parameters¶

min_v (double)

The lower bound. Any element below this is replaced by min_v.

max_v (double)

The upper bound. Any element above this is replaced by max_v. Must be >= min_v.

Both overloads take the bounds as plain scalars only — unlike clamp_min()/clamp_max(), clamp() does not currently have a Series-bound (per-element/broadcast bound) overload. When each element needs its own lower and upper bound, compose clamp_min(lo_series).clamp_max(hi_series) instead.

Returns¶

Series or Series& The bounded result, either as a fresh value (clamp()) or as the mutated current series (clamp_()).

Gradient¶

clamp() is differentiable. Gradient flows to self only where the element was left unchanged by the bound — that is, where min_v <= self[i] <= max_v — and is zero everywhere the element was actually clamped.

Note

Inclusive boundaries on both sides At self[i] == min_v or self[i] == max_v, the derivative with respect to self[i] is 1, not 0 — both boundaries are treated as “inside” the unclamped region. This matches clamp_min()’s and clamp_max()’s own inclusive-boundary convention exactly, which is expected since clamp() is defined in terms of them. See Example 2.

clamp_() is a storage mutation, not a differentiable node — use the out-of-place clamp() when the bound itself needs to sit on the differentiable path.

Examples¶

Example 1. A two-sided bound in one call.

auto line = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 5.0}, {5});

std::cout << line.clamp(-1.0, 2.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, -1, 0, 2, 2]

The two strictly-outside values (-3 and 5) get pulled to the nearest bound; everything already inside [-1, 2] (including the boundary value -1 itself) passes through unchanged.

Example 2. Both boundaries keep gradient 1; only the strictly-clamped positions get gradient 0.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 5.0}, {5});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.clamp(-1.0, 2.0);
y.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, -1, 0, 2, 2]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 1, 1, 0]

Position 1 sits exactly at min_v and position 3 sits exactly at max_v — both keep derivative 1. Only positions 0 and 4, strictly outside the bounds, get derivative 0.

Example 3. clamp_() mutates the current handle in place.

auto line = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 5.0}, {5});
line.clamp_(-1.0, 2.0);

std::cout << line;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, -1, 0, 2, 2]

Example 4. min_v > max_v throws instead of silently swapping the bounds.

auto line = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 5.0}, {5});

try {
  auto out = line.clamp(2.0, -1.0);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << e.what();
}

Output¶

clamp_: min must be <= max

The error is reported under the clamp_ name even when called through the out-of-place clamp() entry point — both overloads share the same bound validation.

Example 5. clamp(lo, hi) and the composed clamp_min(lo).clamp_max(hi) form agree exactly.

auto line = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 5.0}, {5});

auto composed = line.clamp_min(-1.0).clamp_max(2.0);
auto direct = line.clamp(-1.0, 2.0);

std::cout << "composed=" << composed << "\n";
std::cout << "direct=" << direct;

Output¶

composed=pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, -1, 0, 2, 2]
direct=pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, -1, 0, 2, 2]

Notes¶

  • clamp() is the two-sided combination of clamp_min() and clamp_max() — reach for the one-sided methods directly when only one bound applies, and for clamp() when both do.

  • Unlike clamp_min()/clamp_max(), there is currently no Series-bound (per-element) overload of clamp() itself; compose the two one-sided methods for that case.

  • min_v > max_v throws rather than silently producing an empty or inverted range — validate bounds before calling if they come from untrusted input.

  • Use clamp_() when storage mutation is the goal; use clamp() when the bound itself needs to participate in a differentiable computation.

See Also¶

  • Series::clamp_min: the one-sided floor, with a Series-bound (broadcastable) overload clamp() doesn’t have.

  • Series::clamp_max: the one-sided ceiling, with the same broadcastable overload.

  • Series::minimum / Series::maximum: the underlying elementwise comparisons clamp_min/clamp_max are built from.
